denial_rationale: Sepsis-3/SOFA score increase of 2 or more not met
reusable_rebuttal: The patient presented with clinical indicators that supported the claim as submitted and met widely accepted Sepsis-2 criteria. Sepsis was clinically supported when a known or suspected infection was present with at least two SIRS findings, such as fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, leukocytosis, or leukopenia. The denial’s exclusive reliance on Sepsis-3/SOFA criteria did not invalidate the treating provider’s sepsis diagnosis because Sepsis-3 was developed to identify higher mortality risk rather than to serve as the only permissible standard for early clinical diagnosis and treatment.
supporting_criteria: Sepsis-2 SIRS plus infection; Sepsis-3 SOFA may support severity when present
key_clinical_indicators: Infection source, fever or hypothermia, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12 or <4, lactate, procalcitonin, cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids
source_basis: File Library sepsis appeal sources, including Sepsis-2 against Sepsis-3 language
search_terms: sepsis SOFA Sepsis-3 Sepsis-2 SIRS infection antibiotics fluids

denial_rationale: UTI resequenced as principal diagnosis because SOFA criteria were not met
reusable_rebuttal: The denial inappropriately reduced the admission to a localized urinary tract infection despite provider documentation and clinical indicators supporting sepsis. Sepsis was supported by the infectious source, abnormal urinalysis or culture data, systemic inflammatory response findings, and treatment directed at systemic infection, including intravenous antibiotics, cultures, fluid resuscitation, and inpatient monitoring. The absence of a payer-selected SOFA threshold did not negate the documented systemic response to infection.
supporting_criteria: Sepsis-2 SIRS plus urinary source; Sepsis-3 organ dysfunction if present
key_clinical_indicators: UTI/pyelonephritis, positive urine culture, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, lactate, AKI, altered mentation, ceftriaxone or other IV antibiotics
source_basis: File Library E. coli/Gram-negative sepsis denial sources

reusable_rebuttal: Severe sepsis was clinically valid when the record linked infection and sepsis to acute organ dysfunction or hypoperfusion. Organ dysfunction could be supported by acute respiratory failure, AKI, encephalopathy, hypotension with MAP below 70, lactic acidosis, thrombocytopenia, bilirubin elevation, or other acute dysfunction temporally associated with infection. The diagnosis should not have been removed when the provider documented sepsis and the record showed acute organ dysfunction requiring inpatient treatment and monitoring.
supporting_criteria: SSC severe sepsis definition; sepsis with organ dysfunction or hypoperfusion
key_clinical_indicators: MAP <70, SBP <90, lactate >2, AKI, acute respiratory failure, encephalopathy, platelets <150k, bilirubin >1.2

denial_rationale: No ABG or insufficient evidence of hypoxemia
reusable_rebuttal: The absence of an ABG did not invalidate acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Pulse oximetry was clinically acceptable to establish hypoxemia, and respiratory failure was supported when the patient had SpO2 below 91% on room air, a P/F ratio below 300, escalation of oxygen support, respiratory distress, increased work of breathing, or need for high-flow oxygen, BiPAP, or ventilatory support. No minimum oxygen flow rate or mechanical ventilation requirement was necessary when the clinical evidence supported impaired gas exchange and active inpatient respiratory management.
supporting_criteria: Pinson respiratory failure criteria; SpO2 <91% RA; P/F <300; pulse oximetry acceptable surrogate
key_clinical_indicators: SpO2 <91% on room air, P/F <300, S/F <300, Optiflow/HFNC, BiPAP, tachypnea, respiratory distress, increased work of breathing

diagnosis_name: Acute and chronic respiratory failure with hypoxia
denial_rationale: Chronic oxygen baseline or oxygen requirement not high enough
reusable_rebuttal: Acute on chronic hypoxic respiratory failure was supported when the patient’s oxygenation worsened beyond baseline or required acute inpatient respiratory management. A chronic home oxygen requirement did not preclude an acute component. The diagnosis was supported by desaturation on usual oxygen or room air, escalation above baseline oxygen requirement, respiratory distress, tachypnea, labored breathing, S/F or P/F impairment, BiPAP/HFNC use, and treatment of the acute pulmonary process.
supporting_criteria: Acute change from baseline oxygenation; SpO2 <91% on usual FiO2; S/F or P/F impairment
key_clinical_indicators: Home oxygen baseline, increased liters above baseline, SpO2 <91%, respiratory distress, pneumonia, COPD, pleural effusion, HFNC/BiPAP

denial_rationale: KDIGO criteria not met or creatinine rise attributed to CKD/dehydration
reusable_rebuttal: AKI was clinically valid when the record showed a creatinine rise meeting KDIGO criteria, including an increase of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, an increase to at least 1.5 times baseline within the prior seven days, or qualifying oliguria. The diagnosis was further supported when clinicians treated and monitored renal dysfunction with IV fluids, strict intake and output, avoidance or holding of nephrotoxins, medication adjustment, renal trend surveillance, or renal imaging consideration. CKD or dehydration did not invalidate AKI when an acute renal change was documented and treated.
key_clinical_indicators: Baseline creatinine, peak creatinine, 0.3 mg/dL rise in 48 hours, 1.5x baseline, oliguria, IV fluids, held Lasix/lisinopril/nephrotoxins

denial_rationale: Baseline dementia or delirium only; toxic etiology not supported
reusable_rebuttal: Encephalopathy was supported when the record documented an acute global alteration in mental status beyond baseline with confusion, disorientation, hallucinations, inability to provide history, inattention, or fluctuating mentation, and the provider linked the condition to an acute systemic cause such as infection, renal failure, medication, or toxin exposure. Baseline dementia did not exclude superimposed encephalopathy when the record showed an acute change that improved with treatment of the underlying condition.
supporting_criteria: Acute encephalopathy as global functional alteration in mental status due to systemic factor
key_clinical_indicators: Acute confusion, disorientation, hallucinations, altered level of consciousness, baseline comparison, infection, renal failure, provider query response, improvement with treatment

denial_rationale: Payer required weight loss, low BMI, or severe muscle deficit only
reusable_rebuttal: Severe malnutrition was clinically validated when the registered dietitian documented at least two ASPEN characteristics in the appropriate clinical context. The diagnosis did not require the payer’s narrower combination of low BMI, severe weight loss, and severe muscle deficit when ASPEN allowed diagnosis using characteristics such as insufficient energy intake, weight loss, loss of muscle mass, loss of subcutaneous fat, fluid accumulation, or reduced grip strength. The record supported reporting when the provider accepted or documented severe malnutrition and the care plan included nutrition intervention, supplements, intake goals, and monitoring.
supporting_criteria: ASPEN/Academy malnutrition characteristics; at least 2 of 6 characteristics
key_clinical_indicators: Intake <=50% for >=5 days, weight loss, moderate muscle loss, fat loss, edema/fluid accumulation, reduced grip strength, RD assessment, oral supplements

denial_rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria or UTI syndrome not supported
reusable_rebuttal: Acute cystitis or UTI was supported when the record documented a compatible urinary syndrome with objective urine findings and treatment. Useful support included dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, CVA pain, fever, leukocytosis, acute functional decline or mental status change without a better alternate cause, pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and a qualifying urine culture. Antibiotic treatment, urine culture follow-up, catheter management, and provider documentation strengthened validation.
supporting_criteria: SHEA/IDSA-style symptomatic UTI criteria; urinary symptoms plus pyuria/culture
key_clinical_indicators: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, CVA tenderness, fever, leukocytosis, pyuria, nitrites, leukocyte esterase, culture >=100,000 CFU/mL

MRSA or bacterial pneumonia remained clinically valid when supported by provider documentation, respiratory culture or diagnostic evidence, broad-spectrum antibiotics such as vancomycin and Zosyn, CDI query confirmation when present, and acute organ dysfunction such as hypoxia.
